entry: Graphical method for summarizing the distribution of numerical data by its quartiles. The box runs from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3), with a line marking the median. Whiskers extend from the box to show variability beyond the quartiles, and outliers may be plotted as individual points. Box plots are non-parametric, though Tukey's version assumes symmetry for the whiskers. John Tukey introduced the box-and-whisker plot in 1970.

Anti-foreign uprising in North China, 1899–1901, at the end of the [[Qing dynasty]]. Its members, the Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists, were called "Boxers" in English because many practiced [[Chinese martial arts]]. Following the [[First Sino-Japanese War]], villagers resented foreign spheres of influence and Christian missionaries. Beginning in 1899 the movement spread across [[Shandong]] and the [[North China Plain]], destroying railroads and attacking Chinese Christians and missionaries. In June 1900 Boxer fighters converged on Beijing. [[Empress Dowager Cixi]] supported the Boxers and issued an imperial decree that was a de facto declaration of war on the invading powers. An Eight-Nation Alliance of foreign powers defeated the imperial army at [[Tianjin]], reached Beijing on August 14, 1900, and relieved the 55-day siege of the Legation Quarter. The Boxer Protocol of September 7, 1901, required the execution of officials who had supported the Boxers, foreign troops in Beijing, and an indemnity of 450 million taels of silver over 39 years.

Combat sport and martial art involving punching in a ring over timed rounds. Boxers wear protective gloves, hand wraps and mouthguards. The term usually refers to the Western style, but it also covers striking sports such as [[Kickboxing|kickboxing]] and [[Muay Thai]], which may allow kicks and elbow strikes. Boxing may date to the 6th millennium BC in what is now [[Ethiopia]], and was adopted in Egypt from [[Nubia]] before spreading to [[Ancient Greece]] and Rome. It was added to the [[Olympic Games]] in 688 BC. The modern sport developed from 16th- to 18th-century prizefights in Great Britain and the Marquess of Queensberry Rules of 1867. A referee oversees rounds of one to three minutes; a bout is decided by knockout, stoppage or judges' scorecards. Repetitive head trauma is linked to [[Chronic traumatic encephalopathy|chronic traumatic encephalopathy]].

Holiday on December 26, the day after Christmas, observed in the [[United Kingdom]] and several Commonwealth nations. It was once a day for giving gifts to those in need and has become part of [[Christmas]] festivities. Giving money or gifts to people in service positions has been dated to the [[Middle Ages]]. The name may derive from "Christmas boxes," gratuities tradesmen collected on the first weekday after Christmas. A bank holiday may fall on December 27 or 28 to ensure a weekday. In parts of Europe, December 26 is St. Stephen's Day, the second day of Christmas.

Young male human, usually a child or adolescent. A boy becomes a [[Man|man]] on reaching adulthood. The word comes from Middle English *boi*, *boye* ("boy, servant"), though its exact etymology is obscure. A boy typically develops from an XY chromosome pair, and testosterone produced by the male embryo at about nine weeks' gestation drives development of the male reproductive system. Boys typically begin [[Puberty|puberty]] at ages 11–12 and complete it at 16–17, with enlargement of the testicles and scrotum first. Since 1821, in the United States and South Africa, "boy" has been used as a disparaging term for men of color, especially Black men, implying subservient status.

Member of the highest rank of the feudal nobility in many Eastern European states. Comparable to dukes, boyars were second only to ruling princes, grand princes or tsars from the 10th to the 17th centuries. The rank existed in Bulgaria, [[Kievan Rus']] (later Russia), Moldavia, [[Wallachia]] (later [[Romania]]), [[Lithuania]] and among Baltic Germans. In Kievan Rus', boyars held the highest state offices and advised the grand duke through a council, the *duma*. They received extensive land grants and were the major legislators of Kievan Rus'. After the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, boyars from western and southern Rus' were absorbed into Lithuanian and Polish nobility.

Empirical gas law describing the relationship between [[Pressure|pressure]] and [[Volume|volume]] of a confined gas. At constant temperature and for a fixed amount of gas, the pressure of an ideal gas is inversely proportional to the volume it occupies, so their product is constant. [[Robert Boyle]] published the law in 1662 after experiments with air in a closed J-shaped tube. The French physicist Edme Mariotte discovered the same relationship independently, so the law is also called Mariotte's law.

Form-fitting [[Underwear|underwear]] primarily used to support and cover a woman's [[Breast|breasts]]. A typical bra has a chest band, two breast cups and shoulder straps, and usually fastens at the back with a hook and eye. Styles include nursing bras for [[Breastfeeding|breastfeeding]] and sports bras for exercise. Garments supporting the breasts were worn in [[Ancient Greece]], but the first modern bra was made in 1913 by Mary Phelps Jacob from two handkerchiefs and ribbon. After she patented the design in 1914, she briefly manufactured bras in a two-woman factory in [[Boston]], then sold the patent to the Warner Brothers Corset Company, which began mass production. The bra largely replaced the corset in the first half of the 20th century. Most Western women wear bras.

Mathematical notation for linear algebra and linear operators on complex [[Vector space|vector spaces]], designed for calculations in [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. [[Paul Dirac]] introduced it in his monograph *The Principles of Quantum Mechanics*, published by Oxford University in 1930; the name comes from the English word *bracket*. A ket |v⟩ denotes a vector representing a quantum state. A bra ⟨f| denotes a linear form that maps a vector to a complex number, written ⟨f|v⟩. For ℂⁿ, kets are column vectors and bras are row vectors, and combinations are computed by [[Matrix multiplication|matrix multiplication]].

Genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in [[North America|North America]] during the Late Jurassic, about 155.6 to 145.5 million years ago. Elmer S. Riggs described it in 1903 from fossils found in the [[Colorado River]] valley in Colorado. Its forelimbs were longer than its hindlimbs, giving it a steeply inclined trunk and allowing it to browse vegetation as high as 9 meters (30 ft) off the ground. Estimated at 18–22 meters long, it was once thought to be one of the largest dinosaurs. It appeared in the 1993 film *Jurassic Park*. Most popular depictions are based on *Giraffatitan* from [[Tanzania]].

Infraorder of decapod crustaceans comprising the [[Crab|true crabs]]. They have a very short abdomen usually hidden under the thorax, a thick exoskeleton and five pairs of legs, the frontmost ending in pincer-like chelae. True crabs live in all the world's oceans, in fresh water and on land. They are omnivores, eating a significant proportion of algae as well as detritus and other invertebrates, and over 1.5 million tonnes are caught annually for food. True crabs first appeared in the fossil record during the Jurassic period, around 200 million years ago, and diversified in the Cretaceous. Around 7,000 living species in 96 families are known. Females brood fertilized eggs on their abdomen until the zoea larvae hatch into the plankton.

Either of two tall punctuation marks, used in symmetric pairs to isolate text or data. Without qualification, *brackets* means round brackets, ( ), in British English and square brackets, [ ], in American English. Angle brackets, or chevrons, were the earliest type to appear in written English. Erasmus coined the term *lunula* for round brackets. Braces first became part of a character set with the 8-bit code of the IBM 7030 Stretch. [[ASCII]] in 1961 included parentheses, square and curly brackets. In mathematics, brackets denote specific functions and set the [[Order of operations|order of operations]].

Water with more salinity than freshwater but less than seawater. It results from mixing seawater and fresh water, as in [[Estuary|estuaries]], or occurs in brackish fossil aquifers. Technically it contains 0.5 to 30 grams of salt per liter, and water above 30 parts per thousand is considered saline. Estuaries are the most extensive brackish habitats worldwide. Human activities such as dikes and flooding coastal [[Marsh|marshland]] can produce brackish water, which is hostile to the growth of most terrestrial plants.

American actor and film producer. Pitt first gained recognition as a cowboy hitchhiker in the road film *Thelma & Louise* (1991), directed by [[Ridley Scott]]. He became a leading star in films such as *Fight Club* (1999), the *Ocean's* trilogy (2001–2007) and *Inglourious Basterds* (2009). He received Academy Award nominations for *12 Monkeys* and *Moneyball*, and won Best Supporting Actor for playing a stuntman in *Once Upon a Time in Hollywood* (2019), directed by [[Quentin Tarantino]]. As a producer, he won Best Picture for *12 Years a Slave* (2013). His marriages to [[Jennifer Aniston|Jennifer Aniston]] and [[Angelina Jolie|Angelina Jolie]] attracted widespread media attention.

American actor and filmmaker. Cooper's breakthrough came with the comedy *The Hangover* (2009). He has been nominated for twelve [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for films including *Silver Linings Playbook*, *American Hustle*, *American Sniper*, *A Star Is Born* and *Maestro*. For *A Star Is Born*, which he also wrote, directed and starred in, he earned a BAFTA Award and two Grammy Awards. He voiced Rocket in six films of the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]]. On stage, he portrayed Joseph Merrick in a Broadway revival of *The Elephant Man*. He was named People magazine's Sexiest Man Alive in 2011.

Creator god in Hinduism, member of the *Trimurti* with [[Vishnu|Vishnu]] and [[Shiva|Shiva]]. He is associated with the creation of everything, knowledge and the *Vedas*. He is commonly depicted with four heads and four hands, representing the four Vedas, seated on a lotus with a swan or goose as his mount. In some *Puranas* he creates himself in a golden embryo called *Hiranyagarbha*. Brahma was prominent in the post-Vedic period but had lost much of his significance by the 7th century. Few temples are dedicated to him in India, the best known being the Brahma Temple in Pushkar, [[Rajasthan]]. A shrine at the Erawan Shrine in [[Bangkok]] is popular with Thai Buddhists. He is not to be confused with the impersonal concept of [[Brahman|brahman]].

Indian mathematician and astronomer, credited as the first to formalize the concept of zero as a number. His *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta* (628), a treatise on mathematics and astronomy, contains the first clear description of the [[Quadratic formula|quadratic formula]]. He also wrote the *Khaṇḍakhādyaka* (665), a practical manual of [[Astronomy|astronomy]] for students. He worked in Bhillamāla in Gurjaradesa and later at Ujjain, a major center for astronomy. His texts were translated into Arabic by an astronomer at the court of Caliph al-Mansur (754–775). His work influenced [[Bhāskara II]].

Metaphysical concept of the unchanging ultimate reality in Hinduism. In the [[Upanishads]], Brahman is that from which all existence proceeds, to which everything returns, and the origin and cause of all that exists. It is a neuter, gender-neutral concept, distinct from the creator god [[Brahma]]. In non-dual schools of [[Vedanta]], such as Advaita Vedanta, Brahman is identical with the substance of *Atman*, the self, which is inside every living being. In dualistic schools such as Dvaita Vedanta, Brahman is different from the *Atman* of each being.

River in southwestern China, northeastern India and Bangladesh. Ninth largest river in the world by discharge and fifteenth longest, it is about 3,000 km (1,900 mi) long. It rises as the Yarlung Tsangpo near [[Mount Kailash]] on the northern side of the [[Himalayas]] in [[Tibet Autonomous Region|Tibet]], and flows through gorges into [[Arunachal Pradesh]]. It is called the Brahmaputra in [[Assam]] and the Jamuna in [[Bangladesh]], where it merges with the [[Ganges]]. Its average discharge is about 22,000 m³/s, and floods reach about 103,000 m³/s. The river is prone to catastrophic spring flooding from Himalayan snowmelt. Its name means "son of [[Brahma]]" in Sanskrit.

Family of abugida writing systems descended from the Brahmi script of ancient India. They are used by languages in South, East, Central and [[Southeast Asia]], including Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman, Turkic and Austronesian languages. Brahmi is clearly attested from the 3rd century BCE under [[Ashoka]], who used it for imperial edicts. Northern Brahmi gave rise to the [[Gupta Empire|Gupta]] script, which diversified into medieval scripts such as Nagari, Siddham and Sharada by the 7th or 8th century. Each consonant has an inherent vowel, usually a short "a", and dependent forms of other [[Vowel|vowels]] attach to it. The tabular order of modern Japanese kana is believed to descend from Indic scripts, most likely through Buddhism.

Varna, or social class, in Hindu society, traditionally the highest of four. The other varnas are the Kshatriya (rulers and warriors), Vaishya (traders, merchants and farmers) and Shudra (laborers). Brahmins traditionally served as priests at Hindu temples, performed rites of passage such as weddings, and served as spiritual teachers. The *Bhagavad Gita* ties varna to a person's qualities, conduct and occupation rather than birth. Within the jati (caste) system, Brahmins occupy the highest position, though other castes have challenged that status. In [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] and [[Jainism|Jain]] texts, "Brahmin" often means a master or guide rather than a caste.

Tactile writing system used by blind and visually impaired people. Braille characters are formed from six raised dots in a 3 × 2 cell, giving 64 possible combinations, including none for a word space. [[Louis Braille]], a Frenchman who lost his sight in a childhood accident, developed the code in 1824, based on the French [[Alphabet|alphabet]]. His system later included [[Musical notation|musical notation]] and was published in 1829. The second revision, published in 1837, was the first binary form of writing developed in the modern era. Braille can be read on embossed paper or on refreshable braille displays, and early braille education is crucial to literacy and employment for blind people.

Permanent, irreversible and complete loss of brain function. It differs from [[Vegetative state|persistent vegetative state]], in which some autonomic functions remain. Brain death is used as an indicator of legal death in many jurisdictions, though it is defined inconsistently. Definitions differ on whether the [[Brainstem|brainstem]] is included, and in some cases spontaneous breathing may continue. Finland became the first European country to adopt brain death as a legal definition, in 1971. Since the 1960s, laws on determining death have been implemented in all countries with active [[Transplantation (medicine)|organ transplantation]] programs.

Destruction or degeneration of brain cells, also called brain damage or neurotrauma. It may result from external trauma, such as accidents or falls, or from internal causes such as [[Stroke|strokes]] or [[Infection|infections]]. Traumatic brain injury (TBI), caused by external physical trauma to the head, is the most common type. Primary injuries occur at the moment of trauma, while secondary injuries develop afterward from physiological responses such as hypoxia and swelling. A mild injury from a blow to the head is a [[Concussion|concussion]]. Symptoms can include headaches, confusion and fatigue, and severe injuries may cause loss of consciousness and long-term cognitive impairment. Treatments include medication, [[Physical therapy|physical therapy]], [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]] and surgery.

Growth of abnormal cells in the brain, either benign or malignant. Primary tumors start in the brain, while secondary tumors are [[Metastasis|metastatic]] and have spread from elsewhere in the body; secondary tumors are about four times as common, and about half come from [[Lung cancer|lung cancer]]. In adults the most common primary types are meningiomas, usually benign, and astrocytomas such as glioblastomas. Diagnosis uses [[CT scan|CT]] or [[Magnetic resonance imaging|MRI]], often confirmed by biopsy. Treatment may combine [[Surgery|surgery]], [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]] and [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]]. The average five-year survival rate for malignant brain cancers in the United States is 33%.
